KEY MESSAGE 1...A few stronger storms are possible, mainly west of 
the CT River Valley today.

A seasonably warm and humid day is ongoing, helping fuel 
thunderstorms from the Mid-Atlantic into the New York City metro. 
However, the threat for severe storms across southern New England is 
decreasing, albeit not zero. This is highlighted by the current 
outlook, which indicates the greatest risk is mainly west of the 
Connecticut River Valley, where a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 5) 
exists. The greatest concern is across the Berkshires and points 
west, where a Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) exists. Driving today's 
weather is a mid-level closed low over southern Hudson Bay and a 
neutral to slightly positively tilted trough. Dynamics are modest, 
with 0-6 km bulk shear around 35 kt, CAPE values of 1,000-1,500 J/kg 
west of the Connecticut River, and effective helicity of 50-100 
m2/s2.

It is a tricky forecast, as there is sufficient instability across 
southern New England, with the greatest CAPE values remaining west 
of a Willimantic-Worcester-Fitchburg line. However, some high-res 
guidance suggests ongoing convection from the Mid-Atlantic into the 
NYC metro may work over the environment to our south, limiting the 
northward transport of higher instability into southern New England 
this afternoon. This could ultimately reduce the amount of 
instability available for storms later today. Nevertheless, any 
storms that do develop will have the potential for gusty winds, 
which remain the primary concern given DCAPE values around 800 J/kg. 
Small hail is also possible, and an isolated tornado cannot be ruled 
out. We continue to feel the greatest risk for any stronger storms 
is west of the Connecticut River Valley.

Today's 12z suite of guidance continues to support storm development 
across New York State by mid-afternoon, reaching western New England 
between 5-8 PM. The greatest risk for stronger storms will be during 
the late afternoon and early evening, primarily west of the 
Connecticut River Valley. Farther east, decreasing instability with 
the loss of daytime heating, marginal mid-level lapse rates around 
5.5-6.5 C/km, and limited moisture should result in a less favorable 
environment. A few storms may survive eastward into central and 
eastern southern New England, but coverage and intensity should 
diminish.

Mild overnight with stratus advecting in from the south, which may 
lead to low clouds and areas of fog mainly across RI into 
southeastern MA. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Spot shower or thunderstorm possible Friday, 
otherwise a mainly dry and pleasant late-summer day.

Clouds early to start Friday, followed by seasonably warm and humid 
conditions. A cold front moves across the region during the morning 
into early afternoon, providing a focus for isolated to scattered 
showers and perhaps a garden-variety thunderstorm. Much of the day 
should remain dry, with any shower or thunderstorm activity brief 
and localized.

The cold front clears the coast Friday evening, with winds shifting 
to the northwest behind it. A more comfortable and less humid air 
mass arrives overnight into early Saturday. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Seasonable temperatures and dry weather this 
weekend.

Nice weekend shaping up for Southern New England as large high 
pressure cell centered over southeast Ontario early Sat shifts 
southeastward through Long Island and offshore by Sunday. Expect 
full sun and good mixing helping to temper dewpoints/humidity levels 
to tolerable levels. Seasonable highs in the upper 70s to low 80s 
with good radiational cooling both Sat and Sun nights supporting 
lows in the upper 50s to low 60s. Enjoy the weather this weekend as 
we turn more active and unsettled starting Monday - more on that to 
follow below. 


KEY MESSAGE 4...Cloudy and unsettled early to mid next week 
with several opportunities for showers and storms, but the 
timing of them is uncertain.

Our weather pattern then turns more unsettled starting Monday into 
midweek, as the northern mid-Atlantic and Southern New England 
remains entrenched between cooler northerly flow over northeast New 
England and a strong surge of warm, humid air on southwest flow over 
the Ohio Valley and Upper Midwest. Quasi-stationary/backdoor sfc 
frontal boundary looks to be draped in vicinity of Southern New 
England Monday thru Wednesday, with embedded hard-to-time shortwaves 
in a fast NW flow in mid-levels, atop the stalled frontal boundary, 
favoring several opportunities for showers and thunderstorms along 
its extent. 

Other than it being a pattern which favors cloud cover and periods

guidance available at this point, confidence in the timing of
